text: We need to establish the game vision. The genre is 2d sidescrolling action game, iron man/permadeath, real-time tactics, strategic campaign, dynamic narrative.

I’ve framed the genre stack as a coherent initial vision rather than treating each label as a separate feature. The central unresolved issue is what permadeath removes: the controlled character, individual squad members, or the entire campaign. That choice will substantially change the action, tactics, and narrative structure.
Accepted a change to the Game Vision

Good work, but there's one change you need to make. It's not one real-time continuous mission. The game does use a level structure. You start in your base in the strategic layer, you choose a mission, get your team ready, then start the mission. When you complete the mission, you return to your base/strategic layer. 

Our main source of inspiration for this game, in all things, is 2012's XCOM: Enemy Unknown.

This correction materially changes the campaign structure, so I’ve proposed updating the Vision’s misleading “One continuous war” pillar and documenting the base-to-mission loop on this page. I’ve treated XCOM: Enemy Unknown as the project’s primary design benchmark, but “in all things” is too broad to function as a literal rule: its turn-based combat and presentation cannot override this game’s established real-time, 2D side-scrolling identity.
Accepted a change to the Game Vision

Another key pillar is that you play with a squad of soldiers, not by yourself. It should be very dangerous to embark on a mission with one soldier. Four should be the regular number, but often you'll field even more.

This establishes squad deployment as a genuine pillar, not merely a preparation option. I’ve proposed making four soldiers the normal baseline while preserving larger deployments and technically possible—but deliberately hazardous—solo missions. The major unresolved issue is what determines squad capacity above four; setting that now would invent a progression rule the conversation has not established.

We don't need to mechanically limit squad capacity yet. If we need to address the question, let's say that there is no cap on squad capacity. You could bring twenty people if you wanted. But there are soft caps: it costs time and money to hire, train, and equip soldiers. And friendly fire is always on, and the game is very deadly, and the levels are not always huge, so extra squadmates are sometimes more hindrance than help.

The squad has no hard deployment cap. Its practical limits are systemic: recruiting, training, and equipment consume campaign resources, while always-on friendly fire, lethal combat, and constrained level space make very large squads increasingly difficult to use safely. This is stronger than an arbitrary capacity rule because the player may overcommit when circumstances justify it—and own the consequences.

The remaining important question is not capacity, but command usability: how the player effectively controls a large squad in real time without removing the coordination pressure that makes extra soldiers risky.

That's a good question that I don't have an answer for. I haven't even considered how the player will control the other squadmates. They will be very autonomous, with relatively capable AI. But the player should be able to give them commands as suggestions. Lert's create a Squad Command page to detail that system.

The campaign loop should treat squad command as a separate mission-level system. I’ve proposed creating [[Squad Command]] and linking this page to it, while narrowing this page’s open questions to the remaining deployment issue. The new page should begin from two firm principles: squadmates act autonomously with capable AI, and player commands are suggestions rather than guaranteed orders. The actual command vocabulary, compliance rules, and control interface remain deliberately undefined.
